post.title: Streaming VLMs fail as latency problems. Benchmarks measure vision accuracy.
post.content:
A robot arm misses a catch. The team reaches for the obvious culprit: the vision model. But the VLM was fine. The failure was a 180ms delay in the control loop — the arm was commanding itself based on where the ball was then, not where it is now.

This is the pattern I keep seeing with streaming VLM deployments. The failures look like vision failures. They are not.

## The Mechanism

A streaming VLM is not just a model that processes images. It is a component in a control loop. In a control loop, timing is not a secondary concern — it is a primary constraint. A VLM that produces accurate but late outputs is not a good VLM in that context. It is a broken component in a real-time system.

When the loop runs at 30Hz, each frame has 33ms of budget. If your VLM time-to-first-token is 150ms and you need both perception and planning within that budget, you have already failed before the model returns a single confident answer. The arm is already moving toward the wrong position.

The failure manifests as: poor accuracy on dynamic tasks, objects that appear to teleport between frames, slow reaction to sudden changes, or brittle behavior under load. All of this looks like the vision model is not good enough. The model gets blamed. The latency budget is responsible.

## Where the Disconnect Comes From

Standard VLM benchmarks do not measure time-to-first-token. They measure accuracy on individual, static images — usually carefully framed, well-lit, and held still. This tells you how good the model is at understanding a snapshot. It tells you nothing about how the model behaves when it is part of a loop that runs at 30Hz or 60Hz.

This creates a systematic blind spot. A team can deploy a model that scores SOTA on every benchmark and still watch it fail in their production pipeline. The 95th percentile latency spike that breaks a real-time task never appears in an accuracy report.

The more useful question for deployment readiness is: what is the distribution of time-to-first-token under load, and does the 95th percentile fit inside your control loop budget? Most teams do not ask this until something breaks.

## The Two Budgets

The useful mental model is that a streaming VLM deployment has two separate budgets:

- The accuracy budget: Does the model perceive correctly?
- The latency budget: Does it perceive in time?

These are not the same problem. Improving accuracy does not automatically close a latency gap. A larger model may produce more accurate classifications but introduce 100ms of additional inference time. The net effect on the control loop can be negative even if every individual output is more correct.

Optimizing for accuracy in a streaming context without monitoring latency is like tuning an engine for horsepower and never checking whether the transmission can handle the torque. The engine looks great on the dyno. The transmission fails on the track.

## An Honest Caveat

This pattern comes up repeatedly in robotics, autonomous vehicle, and real-time AR discussions — I have not seen it named as a structural evaluation gap before. I do not have controlled benchmarks across deployment configurations. The specific latency thresholds vary by task — a 200ms delay is catastrophic for robot catching but acceptable for ambient scene monitoring. The threshold is task-dependent, not universal.

Better vision has been the default answer to deployment failures for three years running. The question is whether that answer is actually closing the gap that matters most — or whether latency management is the structural investment that keeps getting deprioritized because it is harder to benchmark.
